title: Airzone One Ltd. (Feb 2022 TCC) Tax Court Canada Case
subject: Air Quality Monitoring Projects: How the Work Is Carried Out Shows Why It Was Undertaken
summary: Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 29, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED tax incentives. Justice Hogan allowed four of six air quality monitoring projects, holding that how work is carried out may help show why it was undertaken, while routine engineering and standard methods remain ineligible.
metaDescription: Learn about the February 2022 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Airzone One Ltd. and key takeaways for Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Case Overview and Procedural History

On February 21, 2022, Justice Robert J. Hogan of the Tax Court of Canada issued the Reasons for Judgment in Airzone One Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2022 TCC 29 (Docket: 2018-379(IT)G). The decision is a notable development in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence, in which the Court expressly cited the Canada Revenue Agency's (CRA) most recent administrative guidance—the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, dated August 13, 2021—and organized its analysis around the "Why" and "How" factors that determine whether work qualifies as SR&ED.

The Appellant, Airzone One Ltd. ("Airzone"), is a corporation that provides comprehensive air quality monitoring services to government agencies and departments, international organizations, and for-profit businesses, services that Airzone and its predecessor corporations have provided since 1979. Airzone carried out work on three projects in each of its 2014 and 2015 taxation years—six claimed SR&ED projects in total—aimed at developing and refining sampling apparatuses and analytical protocols to detect airborne contaminants. Specifically, the claimed projects across the two taxation years encompassed Optimizing Passive Monitoring of Low-Concentration Compounds (2014 Project #1), which sought to expand Airzone's established detection protocol for low-concentration airborne compounds in residential homes from 44 to 52 compounds within a single protocol; Improving Detection of Highly Reactive Sulphur Compounds (RSCs) (2014 Project #2), undertaken after Airzone was retained in 2014 by a consortium of oil companies to measure the level of reduced sulphur compounds (RSCs) emitted from oil sands operations at ambient locations 20 to 60 kilometres from the oil sands site; Improving Detection of New Airborne Compounds (2014 Project #3), conducted in collaboration with Environment Canada to develop extraction, sampling and concentration protocols for brominated and fluorinated organic compounds found at very low concentrations in Canadian Arctic air samples; and Solving Combustion Issues to Develop Artificial Smouldering (2015 Project #1), wherein Airzone designed a testing chamber to mimic coal piles stored at a shipping terminal that were prone to spontaneous smouldering during summer months and to identify and measure the resulting emissions; Measuring Phosphate Compounds at Low Concentration Levels (2015 Project #2), in which Airzone engineered a solar-powered, self-contained sampling system to collect airborne phosphate particles in sub-Saharan Africa; and Measuring Unknown Emissions in Curing Environments (2015 Project #3), in which Airzone developed a high-temperature test chamber and tested passive monitors to identify unknown emissions from plastic extrusion and paint-curing processes.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue, acting through the CRA, audited Airzone's 2014 and 2015 T661 SR&ED claims and disallowed all six projects in their entirety. The Crown's challenge ultimately rested on the Minister's assumption that Airzone resolved the technical uncertainties in each project by applying standard practices, methods or processes of routine analytical chemistry or engineering used in its field to conduct air quality monitoring. According to the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor, Mr. Melnyk, the work involved optimizing established detection techniques and existing methods rather than developing new methodologies, and did not generate new scientific knowledge or technological advancement. Although the Respondent's Reply also contained factual assumptions challenging how the work was carried out, counsel for the Respondent acknowledged at the end of the hearing that the evidence established that Airzone's work on all six projects satisfied the "how factors," leaving as the sole issue whether Airzone had rebutted the assumption that it resolved the technical uncertainties using standard practices.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

Within the Canadian federal tax regime, entitlement to SR&ED expenditure deductions under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA) and Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127(9) of the ITA is governed by the threshold statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement, while expressly excluding routine data collection, quality control, and routine testing.

In evaluating whether Airzone's six projects satisfied subsection 248(1), Justice Hogan anchored the Court's analysis in the five-question test that originates with Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] TCJ No. 340 (98 DTC 1839), as summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (the parties also referred the Court to cases including Logitek Technology Ltd. v. The Queen, 2008 TCC 145). Under this judicial framework, the Court sequentially examines five cumulative criteria: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

Justice Hogan extended this foundational jurisprudence by mapping the Northwest Hydraulic framework directly onto the CRA's administrative "How" and "Why" eligibility paradigm. Under this synthesis, the "Why" requirement encompasses Questions 1 and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic, addressing why the work was conducted—specifically, whether there existed a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through standard practice and whether the work sought to generate new scientific or technological knowledge constituting an advancement. Conversely, the "How" requirement encompasses Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic, addressing how the work was conducted—specifically, whether the taxpayer formulated targeted hypotheses, tested those hypotheses via a systematic investigation conforming to the scientific method, and documented the iterative process contemporaneously.

Crucially, Justice Hogan articulated an evidentiary principle connecting these two pillars, while stressing that each factor must still be considered separately: how a taxpayer carries out work may demonstrate why such work is carried out. The Court recognized that in a competitive commercial environment, a taxpayer is unlikely to expend scarce technical labour and financial capital executing a rigorous, multi-stage scientific method if a known, routine engineering solution is readily available. Consequently, satisfying the "How" may help tip the balance in the taxpayer's favour on the "Why" where the dividing line between standard and non-standard methods or procedures is blurred.
The Court's Final Holding

Conducting a rigorous project-by-project evaluation based heavily on the viva voce testimony of Mr. Fellin, a founder of Airzone and the sole witness called by the Appellant to describe the work—whom the Court found to be an extremely knowledgeable, credible and reliable witness whose evidence merited considerable weight—Justice Hogan allowed the appeal for the 2014 and 2015 taxation years and referred the matter back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment. The Court held that four of the six claimed projects met the statutory SR&ED criteria—specifically, Projects #1, #2 and #3 in the 2014 taxation year and Project #2 in the 2015 taxation year—finding that the work was undertaken to resolve technical uncertainties that could not be resolved through standard procedures, such as detecting compounds at very low concentrations, overcoming the reactivity of reduced sulphur compounds, and designing a first-of-its-kind airborne phosphate sampling system. Conversely, the Court upheld the CRA's disallowance on the remaining two projects (the artificial coal smouldering project, 2015 Project #1, and the curing-environments project, 2015 Project #3), concluding that those initiatives relied on routine engineering and standard methods and procedures.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While Airzone achieved a partial victory at the Tax Court of Canada by rescuing four projects, the complete disallowance of all six projects at the CRA audit and objection stages—and the permanent loss of two projects at trial—exposes critical legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that frequently undermine Canadian SR&ED claims.
Failure 1: Conflating Routine Engineering and Standard Data Collection with Technological Uncertainty

The primary substantive deficiency that doomed two of Airzone's projects at trial is illustrated by Justice Hogan's rejection of Project #1: Solving Combustion Issues to Develop Artificial Smouldering. In that project, coal piles stored at a shipping terminal were prone to spontaneous smouldering during warm summer months. Airzone was engaged to identify and measure the compounds emitted from the smouldering coal piles. Because the risks associated with spontaneous combustion prevented Airzone and its partner from undertaking direct sampling at the coal face using traditional monitoring, Airzone designed and fabricated a laboratory coal smouldering chamber to artificially initiate and sustain a smouldering reaction, and then sampled the off-gassed plumes.

Justice Hogan disallowed the project on two distinct technical grounds that clarify the boundary between standard engineering and experimental development. First, the Court found that the design of the coal smouldering chamber was based on routine engineering. The Court agreed with the Respondent that the chamber, although a little more sophisticated, was not that different from a home-use barbecue: a heating coal was inserted to start the smouldering process, and apertures controlled the amount of oxygen entering the chamber so that smouldering could occur over a two-hour period without full ignition of the coal; this did not require resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty. Second, once the smouldering process was maintained inside the chamber, Airzone appears to have used standard methods and procedures to identify and quantify the emitted compounds; unlike the 2014 projects, there was no evidence that Airzone had difficulty doing so, as the water generated by smouldering that interfered with continuous monitors was addressed by using integrated samplers, and an existing United States Environmental Protection Agency computer model was then used to estimate exposure around the terminal.

From a legal perspective, Airzone fatally conflated empirical data uncertainty with technological uncertainty. Not knowing the chemical composition of smoke emitted from a specific batch of terminal coal is an uncertainty of fact that is resolved via routine data collection and standard chemical analysis, rather than an uncertainty in the underlying capability of analytical science or technology. Notably, the Court did not rest its conclusion on the statutory exclusions for routine testing or routine data collection in subsection 248(1) of the ITA; rather, it held that Airzone had not demonstrated that the work was undertaken to achieve a technological advancement, because Airzone knew what methods could be used to mimic emissions from a smouldering coal pile and knew how to measure those emissions.
Failure 2: Inability to Map Technical Bottlenecks to the Seven Indicators of Knowledge Insufficiency

In evaluating Question 1 of Northwest Hydraulic (the "Why"), Justice Hogan cited the CRA's eligibility guidelines regarding the seven characteristics of problems that may suggest that existing scientific or technological knowledge is insufficient to resolve a problem. Under this guidance, knowledge insufficiency may be suggested when existing design methods are not applicable, when requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, when too many variables or unknowns interact simultaneously, when parameters or conditions lie outside the normal operating range, when the nature of the problem is evolving dynamically, when baseline data is not readily available, or when interlocking constraints prevent standard engineering optimization.

In the allowed projects—such as Optimizing Passive Monitoring of Low-Concentration Compounds and Improving Detection of Highly Reactive Sulphur Compounds (RSCs)—Airzone successfully proved at trial that existing knowledge and standard methods were insufficient; for the passive monitoring project, the Court expressly found that there were too many variables or unknowns to detect and measure the full slate of 52 compounds and that data on how to extract them was not publicly available. For example, in passive sampling governed by Fick's First Law of Diffusion:
J = −D (dC/dx)

where J represents the diffusion flux, D is the diffusion coefficient, and dC/dx is the concentration gradient across the diffusive barrier, the Court accepted that standard methods and equipment—originally designed for industrial settings where concentrations are thousands to millions of times higher than in residential homes—may reach their detection limits at such low concentrations, and that extraction procedures can cause compounds to co-elute, so that Airzone had to modify its solvent (ultimately carbon disulphide with 5% butanol) and adjust its chromatographic conditions, developing a completely new protocol that succeeded for all but two compounds. Similarly, in the oil sands RSC project, reduced sulphur compounds were highly reactive with any type of media and degraded rapidly, sorbent collection degraded the samples, co-pollutants and natural light interfered at ambient locations, and high hydrocarbon levels interfered with a flame photometric detector; although Airzone's experiments did not succeed in establishing a reliable identification and quantification protocol for the suite of 18 RSCs, the Court held that the work was undertaken to resolve technical uncertainties and advance Airzone's technological knowledge.

In contrast, for the two disallowed projects, the Court found that the work constituted routine engineering and the application of standard methods—for example, in the curing-environments project Airzone merely tried different gaskets until it found one (the commercially available Viton gasket, known for withstanding high temperatures) that did not degrade under heat, and Mr. Fellin acknowledged that Airzone had an "inkling" of the direction it needed to pursue. The evidence on these projects described engineering objectives—such as building a combustion chamber or a high-temperature test chamber—rather than isolating system-level knowledge deficits where standard textbook parameters and established analytical procedures broke down.
Failure 3: Absence of Iterative Hypothesis Formulation and Modification (A "How" Ground the Crown Ultimately Conceded)

Under Justice Hogan's synthesis of the law, when a taxpayer claims that a technological uncertainty existed, the Court examines the "How" (Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic) to verify whether the taxpayer actually behaved as though standard methods were inadequate.

A problematic misconception frequently arises during CRA SR&ED audits regarding the role of "observation and measurement". While CRA reviewers often reject claims on the basis that observation and measurement are routine testing activities, the Tax Court in Airzone One did not rule on this issue, because the Respondent conceded that Airzone's work on all six projects satisfied the "how factors," including Question 3 of Northwest Hydraulic (whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses). Accordingly, the two disallowed projects did not fail for want of iterative experimentation; they failed the "why" factor because the Court found the chamber design and gasket selection to be routine engineering and the emission measurements to rely on standard methods and procedures. Even satisfying the "How" could not tip the balance where the Court was persuaded that Airzone knew in advance how to achieve its objectives using standard methods (the "Why").
Failure 4: Evidentiary Fragility and Over-Reliance on Viva Voce Testimony Over Contemporaneous Records

Question 5 of Northwest Hydraulic mandates that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results be kept as the work progresses. As noted in the judgment, Airzone is a small corporation with limited, multi-tasking staff, and a large part of the day for Airzone's staff is taken up by routine testing of air samples. In enterprises that perform both routine commercial laboratory services and experimental method development within the same facility using the same personnel and analytical instruments, the evidentiary burden to segregate routine operations from SR&ED is exceptionally high.

The CRA's Research and Technology Advisor recommended disallowing all six projects on the basis that the work did not generate new scientific knowledge or technological advancement; the judgment does not attribute the disallowance to deficiencies in Airzone's contemporaneous documentation. At trial, held in December 2021—roughly six to seven years after the 2014 and 2015 work—Mr. Fellin was the only Airzone witness to describe the work, and the Appellant also called the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor, Mr. Melnyk, whose examination was conducted as a cross-examination. Justice Hogan found Mr. Fellin to be an extremely knowledgeable, credible and reliable witness and gave his evidence considerable weight in allowing four projects; the remaining two projects were not lost for lack of contemporaneous records—the Respondent conceded that the "how factors," including the record-keeping factor, were satisfied for all six projects—but because the Court found the work to be routine engineering using standard methods.
Failure 5: Commercial Consortium and Government Retainer Ambiguities

Airzone's projects were frequently initiated in response to external mandates—such as being retained in 2014 by a consortium of oil companies to measure reduced sulphur compounds (RSCs) or collaborating with Environment Canada to develop extraction protocols for new compounds in Arctic air samples—although both of those projects were allowed, and the Court did not address contract payments or government assistance because the parties had agreed on the allocation of expenses and related ITCs among the six projects. When SR&ED claims arise out of third-party service contracts or government collaborations, two severe legal vulnerabilities arise under the ITA. First, if an agreement requires the taxpayer to deliver environmental monitoring data reports rather than develop novel analytical technology, the CRA may characterize the engagement as routine commercial fee-for-service delivery. Second, under subsections 127(9) and 37(1) of the ITA, any amount received or receivable by a taxpayer from a taxable Canadian corporation (such as an oil sands consortium member) or a government authority (such as Environment Canada) for SR&ED requested by or performed on behalf of that payer constitutes a "contract payment" or "government assistance." Such amounts directly reduce the taxpayer's Qualified SR&ED Expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis unless the contract strictly establishes that the customer paid solely for commercial goods or standard data reports at fixed market rates, and that the taxpayer independently undertook and funded the internal analytical R&D at its own financial risk while retaining full intellectual property ownership of the resulting analytical protocols.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement examined in Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 29) against the specific deficiencies that caused the CRA disallowance and partial trial loss, alongside the governing evidentiary standard established by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Legal & Evidentiary Failure (Audit & Disallowed Projects)
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof (2022 TCC 29)

cells: Technological Uncertainty (The "Why" — Part 1)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Question 1; CRA Guidelines ("Why" Criterion)

Conflated empirical data unknowns (not knowing the chemical composition of emissions from smouldering coal piles) with technological uncertainty. Built a coal smouldering chamber that the Court found was based on routine engineering (likened to a home-use barbecue) and measured emissions using standard methods and procedures.

The taxpayer bears the burden of rebutting the Minister's assumption that it resolved the technical uncertainties using standard practices, methods or processes; the CRA guideline characteristics cited by the Court (e.g., too many variables or unknowns, data not readily available, interlocking constraints) may suggest that existing technological knowledge was insufficient.
Technological Advancement (The "Why" — Part 2)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Question 4; CRA Guidelines ("Why" Criterion)

Framed project objectives around commercial deliverables (e.g., sustaining artificial smouldering or delivering monitoring reports) rather than generating new analytical chemistry knowledge that advances the company's underlying technological capability.

The work must be undertaken to achieve a technological advancement, which may include incremental improvements to existing methods or establishing that a tested method does not work—as in the reduced sulphur compounds (RSCs) project, where Airzone's experiments did not yield a reliable protocol yet the work was allowed—rather than simply compiling environmental data.
Hypothesis Formulation (The "How" — Part 1)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Question 2; CRA Guidelines ("How" Criterion)

Not a ground of failure: the Respondent conceded that Airzone satisfied the "how factors," including hypothesis formulation, for all six projects. In the curing-environments project, however, the Court characterized trying different gaskets until one worked as routine engineering rather than the resolution of a technological uncertainty.

Each experimental phase must begin with a clearly defined hypothesis specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty, linking independent system variables to a predicted analytical outcome.
Systematic Investigation via Scientific Method (The "How" — Part 2)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Question 3; CRA Guidelines ("How" Criterion)

Not a ground of failure: the Respondent conceded the "how factors" for all six projects; the disallowed projects failed on the "why" because, for example, once the smouldering process was maintained, Airzone used standard methods and procedures to identify and quantify emissions.

Inferential Doctrine: How work is carried out may help demonstrate why it is carried out. Each factor must be considered separately, but satisfying the "how factors" (systematic investigation through experiment and analysis of hypotheses) may help tip the balance in the taxpayer's favour where the line between standard and non-standard methods is blurred.
Contemporaneous Documentation (The "How" — Part 3)
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Question 5; CRA Guidelines ("How" Criterion)

Not a ground of failure: the Respondent conceded the "how factors," including the record-keeping factor, for all six projects. At trial, Airzone relied principally on the viva voce testimony of its sole witness, Mr. Fellin, whom the Court found extremely knowledgeable, credible and reliable.

While credible oral testimony from a knowledgeable technical lead is admissible and carries substantial weight, contemporaneous records kept as the work progresses must clearly track hypotheses tested, experimental data, and analytical conclusions for each project.
Segregation of Commercial Contracts & Government Collaborations
ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 248(1) (Routine Data Collection vs. Contract Payments)

Not a ground of failure: the projects undertaken for a consortium of oil companies (RSCs) and with Environment Canada (Arctic compounds) were both allowed, and the Court did not address contract payments because the parties had agreed on the allocation of expenses and related ITCs.

Taxpayers must prove that work performed alongside client or government mandates involved independent method development to resolve technological bottlenecks, rather than routine execution of prescribed testing protocols.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their tax advisors can operationalize the holdings of Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 29), the following two industry case studies reconstruct high-risk R&D scenarios that mirror the exact legal, technical, and evidentiary pitfalls examined by Justice Hogan. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, technical documentation, contractual structuring, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Environmental and Metallurgical Emissions Laboratory (Overcoming the "Coal Smouldering Chamber" and Consortium Retainer Pitfalls)
Industry Scenario and Fact Pattern

TerraVanguard Analytical Laboratories Inc. ("TerraVanguard") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Mississauga, Ontario, specializing in industrial hygiene and environmental emissions analysis. A consortium of Canadian base-metal mining corporations retains TerraVanguard to investigate fugitive emissions from polymetallic sulphide ore stockpiles stored at northern marine terminals, which undergo spontaneous exothermic self-heating (smouldering oxidation) during humid summer months. The consortium seeks to determine the emission rates of volatile organo-arsenic and reactive reduced sulphur species released during self-heating.

In its initial posture, TerraVanguard files a single overarching SR&ED project titled "Development of Sulphide Ore Smouldering Simulation Chamber and Emission Profiling." The company claims 1,800 hours of engineering and laboratory technician labour spent designing and fabricating a stainless-steel laboratory reaction vessel with PID-controlled heating mantles and mass-flow humidified air injectors to sustain artificial smouldering of ore samples, followed by collecting gas bags from the chamber exhaust over 90 days to run through standard Gas Chromatography–Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (GC-ICP-MS) protocols to catalogue the emitted compounds.
Diagnosis of Legal Vulnerabilities Under Airzone One Ltd. (2022 TCC 29)

If audited by the CRA or litigated before the Tax Court of Canada in this posture, TerraVanguard's claim faces total disallowance on the exact grounds that defeated Airzone's Artificial Smouldering project. First, designing a heated, aerated reaction vessel to sustain smouldering oxidation utilizes standard mechanical and chemical engineering design methods rather than overcoming a technological uncertainty. Second, once smouldering is maintained inside the vessel, analyzing exhaust gases to identify what compounds the ore emits constitutes empirical data collection using known instrumentation, rather than a technological advancement in analytical chemistry. Third, because the mining consortium funded the study, the CRA will assert that even if any eligible SR&ED occurred, the consortium's fees constitute a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, eliminating TerraVanguard's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step A: Restructuring Project Governance and Scope Segregation

TerraVanguard must immediately bifurcate its internal project governance to sever ineligible commercial engineering and routine testing from genuine experimental development. The corporation should establish a commercial project code (COMM-2026-01) capturing all mechanical design, fabrication, and thermal stabilization of the smouldering chamber, as well as all routine GC-ICP-MS sample runs conducted once an analytical protocol is finalized. Concurrently, TerraVanguard must isolate the true analytical chemistry bottleneck within a dedicated SR&ED project code (SRED-2026-01: Passivation and Cryo-Trapping Protocol for Co-Eluting Volatile Organo-Arsenic and Reactive Sulphur Species in High-SO2 Matrices). Internal accounting governance rules must mandate that time may only be booked to SRED-2026-01 when standard EPA or NIOSH sampling methods fail due to chemical matrix interference or compound degradation prior to detection. Prior to opening SRED-2026-01, the Lead Analytical Chemist must execute an Insufficiency of Standard Methods Benchmark Report documenting that standard Tedlar bag sampling and EPA Method TO-15 failed completely because high concentrations of sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and water vapour (H₂O) in the smouldering exhaust triggered rapid homogeneous oxidation and wall-adsorption of trace volatile arsines (AsH₃ and methylated arsines at 0.1–5 ppbv), yielding <15% recovery.
Step B: Technical Documentation Aligned with the Seven CRA "Why" Indicators

To satisfy Questions 1 and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic and the CRA's "Why" guidelines cited by Justice Hogan, TerraVanguard must structure its T661 technical narrative around the specific characteristics of knowledge insufficiency. Specifically, the technical narrative must demonstrate the inapplicability of existing methods and operation outside normal operating ranges by proving that existing solid-sorbent and canister methods are validated only for ambient dry air with low acid-gas background; under smouldering exhaust conditions, the ratio of interfering acid gas to target analyte exceeds 10,000:1, falling far outside published operating envelopes. Furthermore, the narrative must highlight the governing interlocking constraints: stripping water vapour and SO₂ upstream using alkaline scrubbers or Nafion dryers quantitatively strips or catalytically decomposes the target volatile organo-arsenic compounds, whereas bypassing upstream scrubbing destroys the GC column stationary phase and quenches the ICP-MS plasma. Finally, the technological advancement must be framed not as measuring ore emissions, but as advancing analytical separation science by establishing the thermodynamic and kinetic parameters for a novel two-stage selective silanized cryo-focusing trap that removes >99.5% of SO₂ and H₂O matrices while maintaining >90% recovery of sub-ppb volatile organo-arsenic species.
Step C: Contractual Restructuring to Prevent Contract Payment Clawbacks

To prevent the consortium retainer from disqualifying the claim under subsection 127(9) of the ITA or characterizing the work as routine commercial testing, TerraVanguard must revise its contractual architecture. The Master Services Agreement and Statement of Work (SOW) with the mining consortium must be drafted so that TerraVanguard is contracted strictly to deliver a Commercial Emission Inventory Report quantifying emission factors in mg/tonne of ore for a fixed commercial fee of $185,000. The contract must explicitly stipulate that the consortium is purchasing standard analytical testing outputs, is not requesting or funding R&D, and bears zero financial risk if TerraVanguard incurs cost overruns developing internal laboratory methodologies. Moreover, an explicit intellectual property clause must confirm that any novel analytical protocols, sorbent formulations, or instrumentation modifications developed by TerraVanguard remain the exclusive proprietary trade secrets of TerraVanguard, legally decoupling the internal SR&ED from the commercial service deliverable.
Step D: Experimentation Tracking (Proving the "Why" Through the "How")

Leveraging Justice Hogan's observation that how the work is conducted may help show why it was undertaken, TerraVanguard must implement a structured electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) matrix that captures every iteration of the scientific method as the work progresses in compliance with Question 5 of Northwest Hydraulic.

cells: EXP-01 (2026-03-10)
Coating the pre-trap glass beads with potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) at 5% w/w will selectively neutralize SO₂ via acid-base chemisorption without cleaving the As–C bonds of trimethylarsine (TMA).
Synthesized 5% w/w K₂CO₃ coated borosilicate beads; challenged with synthetic smouldering gas (2,500 ppmv SO₂, 15% v/v H₂O, 5 ppbv TMA, 20 ppbv CH₃SH) at flow rates of 100 mL/min.
SO₂ breakthrough reduced to <1%, but TMA recovery dropped to 22% and methyl mercaptan (CH₃SH) recovery dropped to 8%.

Hypothesis Refuted: High humidity caused deliquescence of K₂CO₃, forming a high-pH aqueous film (pH > 11) that catalyzed oxidative hydrolysis of TMA and ionized CH₃SH. Must abandon alkaline salt scrubbers and hypothesize a hydrophobic molecular sieve separation.
EXP-02 (2026-04-02)
Utilizing a hydrophobic dealuminated Y-zeolite (Si/Al > 80) maintained at −30 °C will kinetically exclude bulky organo-arsenic molecules based on pore-size steric hindrance while trapping polar SO₂.
Packed silanized quartz tubes with dealuminated Y-zeolite (0.74 nm pore aperture); varied trap temperature from −40 °C to 0 °C across 12 test runs using Peltier cooling modules.
TMA recovery improved to 68% at −20 °C, but severe peak tailing and memory effects occurred during thermal desorption; SO₂ co-adsorbed in mesopores.

Hypothesis Partially Modified: Residual silanol (Si–OH) defect sites on the zeolite crystal exterior formed hydrogen bonds with TMA. Formulate next hypothesis: gas-phase hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) end-capping of the zeolite surface combined with a two-stage differential thermal desorption ramp.

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Cleantech and Environmental Sensor Engineering (Overcoming the "Observation and Measurement" and Government Collaboration Pitfalls)
Industry Scenario and Fact Pattern

AeroSense Photonics & Sorbents Ltd. ("AeroSense") is a Canadian cleantech manufacturer based in Calgary, Alberta, developing passive and active environmental air monitoring systems. AeroSense enters into a joint testing initiative with Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) to monitor ultra-low-concentration fluorinated greenhouse gases and perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) in sub-arctic ambient environments.

In its initial filing posture, AeroSense submits an SR&ED claim for a project titled "Field Validation and Calibration of Passive Sorbent Samplers for Sub-Arctic Trace Fluorinated Compounds." The T661 narrative states that AeroSense deployed 120 passive diffusive samplers across three field stations over six months, collected the samplers, extracted the analytes in the laboratory, measured the concentrations, and compared the results against active reference pumps to calibrate the sampling uptake rates.
Diagnosis of Legal Vulnerabilities Under Airzone One Ltd. (2022 TCC 29)

In this posture, the CRA will disallow AeroSense's claim in full based on two fundamental vulnerabilities that commonly arise in SR&ED reviews, although neither was the basis of the outcome in the Airzone One litigation. First, because AeroSense described its work as deploying samplers, measuring concentrations, and calibrating uptake curves, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) will invoke the "observation and measurement" misconception to classify the entire project as routine product validation, calibration, and environmental data collection. Second, the claim suffers from retrospective hindsight bias (post hoc reasoning). As cautioned in Northwest Hydraulic, a decision relied on in Airzone One, what appears routine and obvious after the event may not have been before the work was undertaken. However, because AeroSense's documentation only recorded the field deployment schedule and final calibration curves rather than the underlying chemical mass-transfer failures and systematic laboratory experiments, the taxpayer cannot prove that its observation and measurement activities were tied to a systematic investigation.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step A: Restructuring Project Governance and Isolating Core Experimental Work

AeroSense must restructure its project governance to align with the Tax Court's distinction between routine field monitoring and eligible experimental development. Field logistics, routine site visits, and post-protocol calibration runs must be segregated into an ineligible commercial cost centre (OPS-FIELD-04), except where a specific field deployment is strictly scaled and instrumented as an experimental trial required because sub-arctic atmospheric micro-crystallization cannot be replicated in an environmental chamber. AeroSense must then define the core scientific project under a dedicated SR&ED code (SRED-2026-02: Resolving Non-Fickian Boundary Layer Mass Transfer and Ice-Film Pore Occlusion in Functionalized Mesoporous Polymer Sorbents at Sub-Zero Temperatures). Furthermore, rather than depending primarily on one witness's recollection years later at the Tax Court of Canada, as Airzone did with Mr. Fellin (whose testimony the Court found extremely knowledgeable, credible and reliable) in Airzone One, AeroSense's R&D Director and Polymer Chemist must institute contemporaneous bi-weekly review minutes explicitly linking every observation and measurement campaign to a specific mass-transfer hypothesis.
Step B: Technical Documentation Aligned with the CRA "Why" Framework

AeroSense must rewrite its technical documentation to demonstrate why standard passive sampling theory broke down under the seven indicators of knowledge insufficiency. In standard passive diffusive sampling, the mass of analyte collected (M) over exposure time (t) is assumed to follow a linear relationship based on a constant sampling rate (RS):
M = R<sub>S</sub> × C × t, where R<sub>S</sub> = D × A / L

where A is the diffusive cross-sectional area and L is the diffusion path length. AeroSense must document that at temperatures between −40 °C and −10 °C and ambient PFCA concentrations below 1 pg/m³, standard divinylbenzene-co-N-vinylpyrrolidone sorbents exhibited a 35% variance from theoretical Fickian uptake. The narrative must explain how too many variables and evolving problem dynamics prevented standard engineering solutions: hoarfrost micro-nucleation across the PTFE diffusive membrane dynamically altered the effective porosity (ε) and tortuosity (τ) of the barrier, while cryogenic surface kinetics reduced the sorbent-analyte sticking coefficient, causing volatile fluorinated precursors to rebound rather than chemisorb. Consequently, the technological advancement is defined as generating new polymer surface chemistry and mass-transfer knowledge regarding how perfluoropolyether-grafted hyper-crosslinked polystyrene matrices alter activation energy barriers for adsorption at sub-zero temperatures.
Step C: Structuring the Government Collaboration Agreement with ECCC

To protect the claim from disqualification or expenditure clawbacks resulting from the collaboration with Environment and Climate Change Canada, AeroSense must formalize a non-financial Collaborative Research Agreement. Under this agreement, ECCC provides access to federal meteorological monitoring stations and shares reference active-sampler atmospheric datasets, but pays $0 in financial grants, contributions, or service fees to AeroSense. Because ECCC provides no monetary reimbursement, forgivable loan, or fee-for-service payment, AeroSense's internal labour and material expenditures remain 100% self-funded and immune from government assistance reductions under subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA. The agreement must also clearly delineate technical roles, specifying that ECCC is responsible for routine ambient baseline monitoring using its existing high-volume active pumps, whereas AeroSense is independently conducting experimental trials on its proprietary passive sorbent architectures.
Step D: Experimentation Tracking (Demonstrating that Observation and Measurement Serve Systematic Investigation)

To neutralize the CRA's frequent assertion that "observation and measurement" constitute routine testing, AeroSense must structure its contemporaneous experimental logs to show that every measurement was designed to test and modify a specific hypothesis regarding diffusion kinetics and polymer chemistry.

headers: Resulting Modification of Hypothesis & Sorbent Architecture (Questions 3 & 4)

cells: Phase 1: Pore Architecture Trial (PROT-A1)

Increasing mesoporous volume (20–50 nm pore diameter) via hyper-crosslinking with dichloroxylene will prevent capillary condensation of supercooled water vapour, maintaining linear analyte uptake at −25 °C.

Exposed 15 functionalized resin batches in a controlled cryogenic wind-tunnel chamber (−25 °C, 85% relative humidity, 50 pg/m³ perfluorooctanoic acid). Measured uptake rate (R<sub>S</sub>) via LC-MS/MS at 24h, 72h, and 168h intervals.

Uptake was linear up to 48 hours (R² = 0.99), followed by a sudden 60% plateau between 72h and 168h. BET surface area analysis revealed ice-crystal bridging across the outer 50 µm of the diffusive PTFE screen rather than inside the resin pores.

Hypothesis Refuted & Modified: Sorbent pore volume is not the primary rate-limiting factor after 48 hours; boundary-layer ice nucleation on the diffusive barrier governs mass transfer. Formulate Phase 2 hypothesis targeting superhydrophobic fluorinated siloxane nanostructuring of the diffusive membrane.
Phase 2: Membrane Surface Energy Trial (PROT-B4)

Grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyltriethoxysilane (PFOTES) onto the diffusive membrane will lower surface free energy below 15 mJ/m², preventing hoarfrost nucleation without causing competitive adsorption of target PFCAs onto the membrane itself.

Synthesized 4 silanization grafting densities (0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.0 molecules/nm²). Measured contact angle hysteresis, effective diffusivity (D<sub>eff</sub>), and membrane-retained PFCA fraction via separate solvent extraction of the membrane versus the backing sorbent bed.

Ice nucleation was eliminated at grafting densities ≥2.0 molecules/nm². However, fluorine-fluorine affinity caused the membrane itself to retain 18% of the target PFCA analyte, distorting diffusive flux into the sorbent bed.

Hypothesis Refined (Technological Advancement Achieved): Discovered a critical threshold at 1.5 molecules/nm² co-grafted with short-chain zwitterionic betaine groups that suppresses ice crystal adhesion while keeping membrane analyte retention below 3%, establishing a new low-temperature passive sampling protocol.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 29) provides both a powerful evidentiary shield and a stern cautionary warning for Canadian corporate taxpayers and SR&ED advisors. By formally integrating Justice Bowman's five-question test from Northwest Hydraulic with the CRA's "Why" and "How" administrative guidelines, Justice Hogan confirmed that the two inquiries are not isolated silos. Rather, while each factor must be considered separately, demonstrating a disciplined, iterative scientific method through contemporaneous documentation (the "How" under Questions 2, 3, and 5) may help tip the balance toward a finding that a project faced genuine technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through routine engineering (the "Why" under Questions 1 and 4) where the dividing line is blurred.

Conversely, the disallowance of two of Airzone's six projects underscores that the Tax Court will rigorously police the boundary between technological uncertainty and empirical data collection. When a taxpayer constructs an apparatus using standard engineering principles—such as Airzone's artificial coal smouldering chamber—and subsequently applies established analytical procedures to measure unknown environmental outputs, the work will be disqualified as routine engineering and standard testing. To prevail under the Airzone One standard, Canadian claimants must proactively segregate commercial testing hours from experimental development, structure third-party consortium and government agreements to preserve expenditure eligibility, map technical bottlenecks directly to the seven objective indicators of knowledge insufficiency, and maintain contemporaneous hypothesis-driven experimental logs that render the scientific method self-evident prior to litigation.
